newsitem.title: RUSSIA: SOCCER-SPARTAK MOSCOW SOCCER CLUB DIRECTOR SHOT DEAD.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SPARTAK MOSCOW SOCCER CLUB DIRECTOR SHOT DEAD.

text.p: The commercial director of Russia's top soccer club Spartak Moscow was shot dead near the capital on Sunday in an apparent contract killing.

A police officer, speaking by telephone from the village of Taratovo, about 120 km (75 miles) east of Moscow, said Spartak Director General Larisa Nechayeva was killed, along with another woman, when their car came under fire at noon (0800 GMT).
Their driver was wounded, he said, refusing to give any other details of the incident in the village where the club owns a complex of country villas.
A shocked spokesman for Spartak said he knew nothing about the murder.
"I spoke to her yesterday at the stadium and she was on top form," said Alexander Lvov, adding that he was not aware of any threats towards her.
Spartak regained the top spot in the Russian league from city rivals Dynamo on Saturday by beating Lokomotiv Nizhny Novgorod 1-0.

Nechayeva, number two in the club hierarchy and one the few women involved in soccer management, was in charge of Spartak's finances and sponsorship issues, exposing her to the often sinister and dangerous world of Russian post-communist business.

But Lvov said he had no clues as to who was behind the killing. "I don't think she could be of interest to criminal structures because our club is not involved with shadowy organisations, we only deal with football."

Nechayava, a striking blonde who says she got her job by contacting the club's president with the offer of turning the Spartak into a "superclub", won a series of key sponsorship deals recently which put an end to the club's financial worries.

In an interview with Izvestia daily last month, Nechayava said that Spartak had signed a contract with Japanese audio equipment makers Akai Electric Co Ltd, but that its main backer was Urengoigazprom, part of Russian gas monopoly Gazprom.
"Our main income comes from operations with oil and gas. Special commercial structures have been set up to work for the club," she told the paper, without elaborating.
The killing bore a striking resemblance to the murder in April of the head of Russia's Ice Hockey Federation Valentin Sych, who was the third most influential man in Russian sport.
Sych, 60, was killed near his country home when an unidentified gunman sprayed his car with automatic rifle fire.

He told Reuters in an interview in February that criminal activity in Russian sports was getting worse and that many players and officials were scared by organised crime and faced pressure to aid illegal ventures.
Contract killings of businessmen, bankers and officials have become almost commonplace in Russia. Foreigners have also been targeted, though much more rarely. The culprits are almost never caught.

The American part-owner of one of Moscow's most prominent hotels was shot dead near the building in broad daylight last year and two British businessmen and their families had to be evacuated last week because they had received threats.
